business_model: Flash-sale e-commerce, pivoting to owned-inventory home furnishings

historical_evidence.company: Founded 2011 as a social network for the LGBT community (Fabulis), pivoted in 2011 to a flash-sale design/home-goods e-commerce site. By April 2013 had pivoted again, acquiring German custom-furniture company myFab and pushing into owned-inventory home furnishings under a new brand, Hem.
historical_evidence.market: Flash-sale/deals e-commerce was a crowded, cooling category by 2013 (Gilt, One Kings Lane, Zulily all competing); the home-furnishings vertical Fab pivoted into is capital-intensive and inventory-heavy, a meaningfully different model than its original curated-marketplace approach.
historical_evidence.team: Co-founder and CEO Jason Goldberg remained; co-founder Bradford Shellhammer, who had driven the original curation/merchandising vision, departed the company around the pivot (reported November 1, 2013) and moved to a non-executive advisor role.
historical_evidence.product: Original product was a curated flash-sale marketplace for design goods. The pivot introduced Hem, an owned-inventory custom-furniture line, a substantially different (and more operationally complex) product than the original marketplace model.
historical_evidence.execution: Set out to raise $300M in its Series D but closed only $150M in June 2013 at a reported $1B pre-money valuation — a meaningful shortfall against its own target. Two separate rounds of layoffs followed within five months: 100+ employees cut in July 2013, and 100+ more let go in October/November 2013, on top of earlier cuts — reducing headcount from a peak of roughly 700.
historical_evidence.traction: No specific customer-count or revenue figures were disclosed in the contemporaneous coverage reviewed; the company's own public messaging shifted from flash-sale growth metrics to narrative about the furniture pivot, itself a signal that the original metric set was no longer being emphasized.
historical_evidence.financial: Later reporting (2014) disclosed the company was burning approximately $14M/month before the pivot and layoffs, though this specific burn figure was not confirmed as publicly known as of the November 2013 snapshot date and is flagged as a possible evidence-limitation gap (see benchmark_notes).

future_outcome.outcome_summary: Continued to struggle through 2014; sold to PCH International in 2015 for a small fraction of its former $1B valuation, widely reported as an effective shutdown of the original business.

benchmark_notes.why_included: Provides a genuine, non-hindsight-dependent Very Weak anchor: the distress signals (missed fundraising target, two rounds of major layoffs, a co-founder departure) were all real-time, contemporaneously reported facts as of the snapshot date, not retrospective judgment. Tests whether SIE correctly reads clearly negative public evidence as negative rather than defaulting to a moderate score out of caution.
benchmark_notes.known_ambiguities: The company's own messaging around the November 2013 snapshot emphasized the new furniture-pivot narrative rather than providing clean before/after traction numbers, making the Traction and Financial Health pillars genuinely evidence-thin even though the overall picture is clearly negative — a useful test of whether thin evidence in a company that is nonetheless comprehensively distressed gets scored appropriately low rather than defaulting toward the middle for lack of hard numbers.
benchmark_notes.evidence_limitations: The specific $14M/month burn figure only appears in sources published after the snapshot date (October 2014) and has been excluded from historical_evidence and normalized_facts for that reason, even though it plausibly reflects the same underlying period — flagged rather than backdated. No contemporaneous (pre-snapshot) revenue or customer-count figures were found in the sources reviewed.
